title: Statistics
lines: GRE statistics is about describing a list of numbers: where its centre is, how spread out it is, and where one value sits relative to the rest. You will rarely compute a standard deviation, but you must understand what changes it.
## Mean
- Mean = sum ÷ number of values, so sum = mean × number of values. Work with sums: they turn average questions into simple arithmetic.
- Adding a value above the mean raises the mean; below it, lowers it; equal to it, leaves it unchanged.
> Sofia's mean on four tests is 82. What must she score on the fifth for a mean of 85?
> Sum needed = 5 × 85 = 425. Sum so far = 4 × 82 = 328.
> Fifth score = 425 − 328 = 97.
## Median, mode and range
- Median: the middle value after sorting. With an even count, the mean of the two middle values.
- Mode: the most frequent value (a list can have several modes or none).
- Range: largest minus smallest.
> For 7, 3, 9, 3, 12, 5 find the mean, median, mode and range.
! Always sort before finding a median. The middle of the unsorted list (9 and 3 here) means nothing.
! An extreme value pulls the mean but barely moves the median. In a list with one very large value, the mean is above the median.
## Standard deviation as a concept
- Standard deviation (SD) measures how far values typically are from the mean. All values equal gives SD 0.
- Adding the same number to every value shifts the mean but leaves the SD unchanged. Multiplying every value by k multiplies the SD by |k|.
- Values bunched near the mean give a small SD; values far out on both sides give a large one, even with the same mean and range.
> Which set has the larger SD: {8, 10, 12} or {2, 10, 18}?
> Both have mean 10, but the second set's values are 8 away from the mean instead of 2. Its SD is larger (four times as large).
> For the curious: the eight values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 have mean 5. The squared distances add to 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 32; 32/8 = 4, and √4 = 2, so the SD is 2.
! In QC, compare spreads by eye: you almost never need the formula. Adding a value equal to the mean shrinks the SD slightly; adding a value far from the mean increases it.
## Weighted averages
- Weighted mean = (sum of each group mean × group size) ÷ total size.
- The combined mean lies between the group means, closer to the larger group.
> Class A has 20 students with a mean of 70; class B has 30 with a mean of 80. Find the combined mean.
> Not 75: class B is larger, so the result leans toward 80.
## Quartiles, percentiles and box plots
- Quartiles split sorted data into four groups of equal count. Q2 is the median; Q1 is the median of the lower half; Q3 the median of the upper half.
- Interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle half of the data.
- The pth percentile is a value with about p% of the data at or below it. Q1 is the 25th percentile and Q3 the 75th.
- A box plot shows five numbers: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. The box holds the middle 50%; each whisker holds 25%.
> Twelve values: median = (10 + 12)/2 = 11.
> IQR = 16.5 − 6 = 10.5. A box plot would run from 2 to 23 with the box from 6 to 16.5 and a line at 11.
! A long whisker or a wide part of the box does not hold more values; every quarter holds the same count. Width shows spread, not frequency.
! Percentile is not percent correct. A score at the 90th percentile beat about 90% of test takers; it says nothing about how many questions were right.
## The normal distribution
- A normal distribution is a symmetric bell curve; mean, median and mode are equal and sit at the centre.
- About 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SD, and about 99.7% within 3 SD.
- So about 34% lie between the mean and 1 SD above, about 13.5% between 1 and 2 SD above, and about 2.5% above 2 SD.
> Scores are normally distributed with mean 500 and SD 100. About what percent are between 500 and 700? Above 700? What percentile is 600?
> 700 is 2 SD above the mean: half of 95% is 47.5% between 500 and 700.
> 600 is 1 SD above: 50% + 34% = 84th percentile.
! The 68-95-99.7 figures are approximate. Pick the choice described as "about" and do not over-compute.
## Frequency distributions
- A frequency table lists each value and how many times it occurs. The number of data points is the sum of the frequencies, not the number of rows.
- Mean = sum of (value × frequency) ÷ total frequency. For the median, use running totals to find the middle position.
> Ratings: 1 (3 people), 2 (5 people), 3 (8 people), 4 (4 people). Find the mean and median.
> The median is the mean of the 10th and 11th values. Running totals: 3, 8, 16, so positions 9 to 16 are all 3. Median = 3. Mode = 3.
## Shortcuts and timing
- For "what new value keeps the mean the same" questions, the answer is the mean itself.
- For an evenly spaced list, mean = median = (first + last)/2.
- Use the calculator for a long weighted sum, but set up the sums first; most statistics QC questions need no calculation at all.
> Quantity A: the mean of 31, 32, 33, …, 49. Quantity B: the median of the same list.
> The list is evenly spaced, so the mean and median are both (31 + 49)/2 = 40. The quantities are equal.
